Field studies of the Spring peeper (Pseudacris crucifer) have documented key early life history parameters under controlled laboratory conditions. When eggs were incubated at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], hatching occurred after approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], a developmental rate consistent with the rapid embryonic development typical of early-breeding anurans in temperate regions. The newly hatched larvae are remarkably small; each neonate has a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], reflecting the modest energy reserves packaged within the egg. This initial mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 2 millimeters, places the species among the smaller hylid propagules. Upon hatching, the endotrophic tadpoles remain associated with the remnants of the gelatinous egg mass for a brief period before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is consequently very short, as the limited yolk supply is rapidly exhausted given the elevated metabolic demands at this incubation temperature.

Larval development in Pseudacris crucifer proceeds through a well-defined sequence of Gosner stages, culminating in metamorphosis. At a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 100 days , a larval period that is moderately long for a North American hylid. This duration is influential in determining the timing of juvenile recruitment into the terrestrial environment. The aquatic tadpoles are primarily herbivorous, grazing on periphyton and detritus, and their growth trajectory is strongly modulated by both temperature and food availability. Following metamorphic climax, which involves tail resorption and limb bud development, the terrestrial juveniles, or froglets, emerge from the breeding ponds. These recently metamorphosed individuals weigh considerably less than adults and face high predation pressure during their first season on land. The transition from an aquatic to a terrestrial lifestyle necessitates significant physiological restructuring, including skin keratinisation and the shift from gill to lung respiration, all of which are energetically expensive processes.

Sexual maturation in female Spring peepers is a protracted process that extends well beyond the first year of terrestrial life. Under thermal conditions of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females attain puberty at approximately 912 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 912 days following metamorphosis]. This extended juvenile period, lasting nearly two and a half years post-metamorphosis, is notable for a species of such small body size. During this time, the growing juveniles accumulate resources and undergo gonadal maturation, with gametogenesis initiating well before the first breeding season. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 5 grams [Wwi = approximately 5 grams], although individual mass can vary between 3 and 5 grams depending on local habitat quality and prey availability. This relatively modest adult mass, compared to other hylids, influences many aspects of the species' ecology, including calling behavior, fecundity, and susceptibility to desiccation. The adult females are capable of storing sperm, a reproductive strategy that allows for asynchronous fertilisation of successive egg clutches.

The maximum lifespan of Pseudacris crucifer has been a topic of some debate, with the AnAge database providing a probable underestimate of 4 years for wild populations. Recent field recapture data from a long-term mark-recapture study in Virginia, however, indicate that individuals can survive for up to 7 years [am = up to 7 years] when maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] under semi-natural conditions, a longevity that is remarkably high for such a small anuran. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across several breeding seasons. Reproductive output in this species is considerable; females lay between 700 and 1,000 eggs per year [Ri = between 700 and 1,000 eggs per year], distributed across multiple clutches deposited over the extended breeding season. The maximum clutch frequency observed in the field is approximately 1.9 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.9 clutches per year], with individual clutches containing between 200 and 500 eggs [N_R_i = clutches containing between 200 and 500 eggs]. These values, collected at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], highlight the species' high reproductive investment despite its diminutive size.

Metabolic investigations have quantified the energetic costs of maintenance and activity in this species. Respirometry trials conducted at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour] for adult individuals. This exceedingly low oxygen consumption rate is characteristic of small-bodied ectotherms with a relatively sedentary lifestyle outside of the breeding season. The value is consistent with the general allometric relationship between body mass and metabolic rate observed across the Hylidae. During the breeding season, however, metabolic demands increase substantially due to the energetic costs of vocalisation and amplexus in males, and oogenesis in females. The mass-specific metabolic rate of this species is comparable to that of other temperate-zone treefrogs of similar body size. These physiological measurements, combined with the demographic parameters described above, paint a picture of a species that combines a low routine metabolic expenditure with a relatively long lifespan and a moderate-to-high annual reproductive output, a life-history strategy that has proven successful across a wide geographic range.
